assessedOutcomes.mloStatement: MLO 1 [create]: Create an end-to-end HR operations runbook integrating recruitment, onboarding, payroll, and controls for a monthly cycle (Linked PLOs: PLO1, PLO2, PLO3)
MLO 2 [analyse]: Analyse and prioritise conflicting operational tickets to meet service levels while mitigating compliance risks (Linked PLOs: PLO2, PLO3)
MLO 3 [evaluate]: Evaluate control checkpoints embedding GDPR and right-to-work compliance in the runbook, justifying decisions (Linked PLOs: PLO1, PLO2, PLO5)

brief.studentFacingIntro: This in-person simulation assesses your ability to design and operate an integrated monthly HR cycle. You will produce an end-to-end HR operations runbook, triage and prioritise a live-style queue of operational tickets, and evaluate the control checkpoints that embed GDPR and right-to-work compliance. You will submit a concise portfolio and deliver a short in-class presentation explaining your approach and justifying your operational and compliance decisions.
brief.workplaceContext: You are the HR Operations Associate for a mid-sized UK company (c. 350 employees) on a monthly payroll. The business is entering a busy month with multiple starters, a few leavers, and several job offers to be processed. The HR service desk has a mixed queue of recruitment logistics, onboarding tasks, payroll changes, and data updates with conflicting priorities. An internal audit is scheduled soon, with attention on GDPR and right-to-work controls. You must keep service levels on track, prevent compliance breaches, and ensure the monthly cycle runs smoothly end-to-end.
stepByStepInstructions: Attend the kickoff workshop and review the simulation pack (ticket list, mock employee data snippets, policy extracts, and templates). Ask clarifying questions in class.
Map the monthly HR operations cycle from recruitment logistics through onboarding to payroll cut-off and approval. Identify handoffs, inputs/outputs, timings, and points where records are updated.

Create the HR Operations Runbook that integrates recruitment, onboarding, payroll, and control activities for the month. Include a clear process flow and a simple month calendar/sequence showing when key actions occur.

Complete the Ticket Triage Log using the provided ticket set. Categorise, prioritise, and schedule actions to meet service levels. Record rationale for each decision, including risk and dependency considerations, and note any escalations.

Evaluate where GDPR and right-to-work checkpoints must occur within the runbook. Justify why each control is placed where it is, what evidence is retained, and how it reduces risk. Update the runbook to embed these checkpoints.
Prepare an 8-minute presentation (with up to 2 minutes for Q&A) summarising your runbook, ticket triage approach, and compliance checkpoints. Rehearse in class time and seek formative feedback.

Submit your printed portfolio at the start of your presentation session and upload digital copies to the LMS by the stated deadline. If working as a group (2–3 students), include a contribution statement signed by all members.
deliverables: HR Operations Runbook covering the monthly cycle with integrated recruitment, onboarding, payroll, and control steps (including a one-page process flow and a simple monthly sequence).
Ticket Triage Log with prioritisation, scheduling, and rationale for the provided ticket set, highlighting service level and compliance risk considerations.
Compliance Checkpoint Evaluation Note justifying GDPR and right-to-work control placement and evidence requirements within the runbook.
In-class presentation (8 minutes + 2 minutes Q&A) with a concise slide deck summarising the runbook, triage decisions, and compliance evaluation.
If applicable, a one-page Group Contribution Statement signed by all members (2–3 students).

rubric.criterionName: End-to-end HR Operations Runbook (integration of recruitment, onboarding, payroll, and controls)
rubric.fail: Runbook is incomplete, inaccurate, or not aligned to a monthly cycle. Key domains (recruitment, onboarding, payroll, controls) are missing or disconnected. Sequencing and responsibilities are unclear; unusable for operations.
rubric.pass: Runbook covers recruitment, onboarding, payroll, and control steps with a basic monthly sequence and clear responsibilities. Steps are accurate and usable, with a simple flow that supports execution.
rubric.merit: Runbook is well-structured and integrated across all domains with clear handoffs, timings, and dependencies. Includes a coherent flow diagram and monthly schedule that anticipate common exceptions and cut-offs.
rubric.distinction: Runbook demonstrates a robust, fully integrated monthly cycle with precise sequencing, inputs/outputs, owners, and checkpoints embedded. Shows optimisation of handoffs and cut-offs, clear evidence capture points, and practical usability for real operations.

rubric.criterionName: Ticket Triage and Prioritisation (service levels and risk mitigation)
rubric.fail: Prioritisation is inconsistent or incorrect. Actions do not meet service levels; compliance risks are overlooked. Rationale is absent or unclear.
rubric.pass: Most tickets are correctly categorised and prioritised to meet service levels. Provides basic rationale and scheduling; identifies obvious risks and escalations.
rubric.merit: Consistently applies explicit criteria to prioritise and schedule tickets in line with service levels. Provides clear rationale, manages trade-offs, and records appropriate escalations and dependencies.
rubric.distinction: Applies a systematic, transparent triage method that optimises service level performance while reducing compliance risk. Rationale references impacts, dependencies, and timing; communication/escalation actions are well-justified and sequenced.

rubric.criterionName: Evaluation of GDPR and Right-to-Work Control Checkpoints
rubric.fail: Control checkpoints are missing, misplaced, or not relevant. Justification is superficial or inaccurate; evidence requirements are unclear.
rubric.pass: Identifies relevant GDPR and right-to-work checkpoints and places them at appropriate stages in the runbook. Provides basic justification and evidence to be retained.
rubric.merit: Evaluates adequacy and timing of checkpoints with clear justification linked to risk and obligations. Specifies ownership, frequency, and evidence retention; integrates controls into the runbook.
rubric.distinction: Provides a critical evaluation demonstrating robustness and proportionality of checkpoints. Justification clearly links to UK GDPR principles and right-to-work requirements; anticipates audit needs with defined ownership, frequency, documentation standards, and evidence trails.

brief.studentFacingIntro: This self-study simulation mirrors a UK HR shared service monthly cycle. You will produce a practical, operations-ready portfolio that demonstrates how you would run recruitment logistics, onboarding, and payroll activities while embedding compliance controls. You will prioritise a conflicting ticket queue and justify the control checkpoints you embed. All work must be produced independently and submitted digitally.
brief.workplaceContext: You are the HR Operations Associate in a UK organisation of 350 employees with monthly payroll. It is five working days before payroll cut-off. There are four pre-employment cases progressing, two starters due next month, one leaver, and several change requests in the ticket queue. You must align recruitment logistics (interviews and right-to-work checks), onboarding administration (HRIS setup, contracts, induction scheduling), and payroll actions (starters, leavers, changes, absences) to hit service levels without breaching GDPR or right-to-work requirements. Your manager has asked for an end-to-end runbook that can be used next month, a prioritised ticket log for the current week, and a justification of the controls you propose.
stepByStepInstructions: Download the templates provided in the LMS: HR Operations Runbook Template (DOCX), Ticket Prioritisation Log (XLSX), Control Register (XLSX), and Monthly Cycle Calendar (XLSX).

Scope the monthly cycle: define cut-offs, hand-offs, and SLAs for recruitment logistics, onboarding, payroll processing, and controls. Populate the Monthly Cycle Calendar with key dates (e.g., payroll approval, RTW verification, contract issue, HRIS updates).

Create the end-to-end runbook (MLO 1): map each sub-process (recruitment logistics, onboarding, payroll) using clear steps, inputs/outputs, roles (RACI), tools/systems, and evidence to be retained. Integrate dependencies between processes (e.g., offer acceptance triggers RTW check completion and HRIS setup). Include exception paths (e.g., failed RTW, late manager approvals, missing absence data).

Embed controls in the runbook (MLO 1 & MLO 3): indicate where GDPR and right-to-work checkpoints occur, what evidence is captured (e.g., RTW check copy with date and checker), who approves, and how audit trails are maintained. Cross-reference to your Control Register.

Complete the Ticket Prioritisation Log (MLO 2): list the provided ticket scenarios from the LMS case pack (e.g., new starter bank details missing, RTW expiring, absence correction, address change, urgent payroll correction). Rate each by impact, urgency, compliance risk, and SLA deadline. Produce a priority order, planned actions, escalation paths, and time estimates.

Write the triage rationale (MLO 2): explain how you resolved conflicts between tickets when SLAs or compliance risks compete (e.g., an expiring RTW versus a payroll change). Show how your plan protects service levels and mitigates compliance risk.

Evaluate control checkpoints (MLO 3): complete the Control Register to show control objective, control activity, frequency, owner, evidence, GDPR principle addressed (e.g., lawfulness, data minimisation, storage limitation), and right-to-work requirement. Justify the placement, strength, and monitoring of each control. Include residual risk and any mitigations.

Record an 8–10 minute walkthrough (MP4): screen-record your runbook and logs, explaining your monthly cycle, how you prioritised the ticket queue, and why your controls are appropriate. Ensure audio is clear and add captions/subtitles.
Reference only digital sources used (hyperlinks). Useful public references include: gov.uk guidance on right to work checks, and the ICO Guide to GDPR.

Use the pre-submission self-check in the LMS to confirm: the runbook integrates all three areas; monthly cut-offs and SLAs are explicit; the ticket log shows clear priorities and rationales; controls are mapped to GDPR and right-to-work with evidence and owners; files are correctly named and exported to the required formats; no real personal data is included.
Export and submit all artefacts via the LMS submission portal.
deliverables: End-to-end HR Operations Runbook integrating recruitment logistics, onboarding, payroll, and controls for a monthly cycle (with process maps and RACI).
Ticket Prioritisation Log with SLAs, risk ratings, priority order, planned actions, and escalations.
Triage Rationale explaining conflict resolution and impact on service levels and compliance.
Control Register and Evaluation Report justifying GDPR and right-to-work checkpoints embedded in the runbook.
Recorded walkthrough (8–10 minutes) explaining the runbook, ticket triage, and control decisions.
Reference list with hyperlinks to all digital sources used.

rubric.fail: Runbook is incomplete or inaccurate; key sub-processes (recruitment logistics, onboarding, payroll) are missing or disconnected; monthly cut-offs/SLAs are unclear or absent; controls not embedded; sequencing or responsibilities contain material errors that would risk missed payroll or non-compliance.
rubric.pass: Runbook covers the three sub-processes with a workable monthly cycle; shows main steps, hand-offs, responsibilities, and basic SLAs; embeds essential controls at relevant points; minor gaps or ambiguities that would be resolvable during operations.
rubric.merit: Runbook is fully integrated across sub-processes with accurate sequencing, clear RACI, defined inputs/outputs, realistic SLAs and cut-offs; includes exception handling and evidence requirements; controls are placed logically within the flow and cross-referenced to supporting artefacts.
rubric.distinction: Runbook is operationally ready and optimised: interdependencies and data flows are explicit; workload and timing are balanced across the month; measures (e.g., checkpoints, KPIs) are defined; artefacts (calendars, maps, checklists) are consistent and reusable; design clearly supports reliable on-time payroll and compliant onboarding.

rubric.criterionName: Ticket triage analysis and prioritisation to meet SLAs and mitigate risk
rubric.fail: Prioritisation is arbitrary or incorrect; high-risk or time-critical tickets are missed or misclassified; little or no rationale; proposed actions do not meet service levels or address compliance risks.
rubric.pass: Applies a basic, sensible prioritisation using impact/urgency and SLA deadlines; identifies clear next actions for high-priority items; rationale is present though limited; overall plan likely to meet key service levels.
rubric.merit: Uses a systematic framework (e.g., impact–urgency–compliance) with consistent ratings; resolves conflicts and sequences work to protect SLAs; provides time estimates, escalation points, and rationale demonstrating understanding of trade-offs and risk.
rubric.distinction: Implements a robust triage model with transparent scoring and thresholds; justifies decisions with scenario comparisons and mitigations; shows how the plan preserves service levels and reduces compliance exposure; decision log is precise, auditable, and adaptable to changing volumes.

rubric.criterionName: Evaluation and justification of GDPR and right-to-work control checkpoints
rubric.fail: Control checkpoints are missing, incorrect, or misaligned with GDPR or right-to-work requirements; lacks justification; no clear ownership, evidence, or monitoring; risks unmitigated.
rubric.pass: Identifies appropriate control checkpoints and links them to GDPR principles and right-to-work steps; provides basic justification, owners, frequency, and evidence to be retained; outlines simple monitoring.
rubric.merit: Evaluates control effectiveness and placement within the process, with rationale referencing GDPR principles (e.g., lawfulness, minimisation, retention) and right-to-work evidence; defines monitoring, audit trail, and residual risk with mitigations.
rubric.distinction: Presents a critical, well-supported evaluation comparing control options and justifying trade-offs; aligns controls to organisational policy and audit requirements; defines measurable performance indicators and feedback loops; includes a concise DPIA-style consideration where appropriate.

brief.studentFacingIntro: This hybrid simulation asks you to design and demonstrate a practical, end-to-end HR operations runbook for a typical monthly cycle in a UK context. You will triage a live-style ticket backlog, make evidence-based prioritisation decisions, and embed GDPR and right-to-work (RTW) controls. The assignment mirrors real HR operations work with deliverables you can take into the workplace. You may complete activities in-person or online, and choose a live or recorded presentation.
brief.workplaceContext: You are the HR Operations Coordinator for a UK organisation of 300 employees using an HRIS with integrated payroll interface. Each month includes recruitment logistics, pre-employment and RTW checks, onboarding, lifecycle changes, absence processing, and payroll cut-offs. A shared service inbox generates tickets with SLAs (e.g., 24–72 hours). The Data Protection Officer (DPO) expects GDPR-compliant handling of personal data at each step, and the Finance team requires accurate starters, changes, absences, and deductions by payroll cut-off. Resourcing peaks around mid-month assessment days; payroll cut-off is two working days before month-end; RTW checks must be completed before start dates.
stepByStepInstructions: Step 1 — Orientation and pack: Download the simulation pack from the LMS (ticket backlog, anonymised starter/changes list, policy excerpts, and templates). If attending on campus, you may request printed packs.
Step 2 — Define operating assumptions: State any assumptions needed (e.g., HRIS capabilities, SLA definitions, approval tiers, payroll timetable). Keep these consistent across your work.

Step 3 — Draft the monthly runbook (skeleton): Outline the full monthly cycle integrating recruitment logistics, onboarding and RTW checks, lifecycle updates/absences, and payroll preparation and validation. Include timing, roles, hand-offs, and control points.

Step 4 — Build process views and ownership: Add a simple swimlane or flow diagram, a RACI/ownership table, a monthly calendar with cut-offs, and SLAs per activity. Show dependencies and exception paths (e.g., late starter paperwork or failed RTW).

Step 5 — Triage and prioritise tickets: Use the provided backlog. Classify tickets (type, urgency, impact, compliance sensitivity). Apply a clear prioritisation method to resolve conflicts and meet SLAs. Record justification for each decision in your triage log and propose escalation paths where needed.

Step 6 — Plan a peak week: Create a short plan for a high-volume week (e.g., interview days plus payroll prep). Show how you will sequence work, protect compliance checkpoints, and avoid SLA breaches.

Step 7 — Evaluate compliance checkpoints: Identify and evaluate GDPR and RTW control checkpoints within your runbook. Explain why each control is placed where it is and how it reduces risk. Reference relevant GDPR principles and UK RTW requirements in plain English. Propose proportionate improvements where gaps exist.

Step 8 — Prepare a 6–8 minute briefing: Present the integrated runbook, your prioritisation approach, and key compliance decisions. Choose either: (a) live briefing (in-class or live online) or (b) recorded presentation (MP4 or narrated slides).

Step 9 — Quality assurance and submission: Check consistency between your runbook, triage log, and compliance note. Use the naming convention: Surname_Firstname_IHROS_Assignment. Submit digitally via the LMS. If using the physical option, book drop-off and provide a USB with media files. Keep a backup copy.

Optional peer element (hybrid): Attend a live studio session for peer feedback on your draft runbook; alternatively, post your draft process map to the LMS forum and respond constructively to two peers.
deliverables: Integrated HR Operations Runbook covering the full monthly cycle with process map, RACI/ownership, calendar, SLAs, dependencies, and embedded controls.
Ticket Triage and Prioritisation Log with decisions, rationale, SLA outcomes, and escalations for the provided backlog.
Compliance Checkpoint Evaluation Note explaining GDPR and RTW control placement, effectiveness, and any improvements.
6–8 minute briefing (live or recorded) summarising the runbook integration, prioritisation approach, and compliance rationale.

rubric.distinction: Runbook is comprehensive, logically sequenced, and execution-ready; demonstrates seamless integration of all elements with precise cut-offs, hand-offs, SLAs, and contingency paths; control points are embedded and traceable throughout; artefacts (map/RACI/calendar) align perfectly with text and evidence piloting via sample scenarios.

rubric.merit: Clear prioritisation model applied (e.g., impact/urgency/risk); conflicts resolved with reasoned trade-offs and documented rationale; escalations used appropriately; SLA adherence is planned and evidenced with few exceptions.
rubric.distinction: Systematic, data-informed prioritisation across the backlog; decisions balance service, risk, and effort with transparent criteria; competing demands are sequenced to protect SLAs and compliance; logs show outcomes, learning loops, and improvements to prevent recurrence.

rubric.merit: Controls are well-placed and evaluated against GDPR principles and RTW requirements; justification is clear with proportionate mitigations and evidence of how controls operate in practice; residual risks are identified.
rubric.distinction: Controls are critically evaluated and optimised for effectiveness and practicality; justification references GDPR principles and RTW requirements in context; residual risks, monitoring, and improvement actions are articulated; traceability from control to risk and process step is explicit.

brief.studentFacingIntro: This in-person assignment brings together three practical tasks you will commonly perform in an HR operations role. You will compile an audit-ready compliance pack, use onboarding feedback to redesign induction communications and schedule with inclusion in mind, and evaluate an HR metrics dashboard to brief leadership. You will submit a printed portfolio and present your dashboard recommendations in class.
brief.workplaceContext: You are the HR Coordinator in a UK-based SME preparing for an external HR audit in four weeks. The HR Director has asked you to ensure policies and evidence are audit-ready, to respond to recent onboarding survey feedback by improving induction communications and schedule, and to review the HR metrics dashboard ahead of a leadership meeting.
stepByStepInstructions: Plan your portfolio: create a contents page and a clear filename and version label for each artefact.
Compliance pack – scope and inventory: list all current HR policies and key procedures relevant to audit (e.g., right to work, data protection, absence, health and safety, induction).
Build a policy register: record title, owner, approver, version, effective date, next review date, legal/regulatory basis, location, and status.

Create evidence logs: design logs for critical controls (e.g., right-to-work checks, GDPR/UK data protection training completion, DSE assessments, absence documentation). Include sample, anonymised entries that demonstrate how evidence is captured and checked.

Apply version control: create a document control table and demonstrate at least two controlled document versions (e.g., policy or template) with naming conventions, change summaries, approval signatures/dates.
Quality check for audit-readiness: verify completeness, traceability, and sampling readiness. Note any gaps and mitigations in a short summary note.

Analyse onboarding feedback: review the provided survey results, FAQs and email threads. Identify themes, bottlenecks, and accessibility/inclusion issues (e.g., clarity, timing, readability, format, reasonable adjustments).
Redesign induction communications: draft two improved templates (e.g., pre-start welcome email and Day 1 joining instructions) and update an FAQ section that addresses common queries inclusively.

Create an inclusive induction schedule: produce a clear timetable for the first 2–4 weeks (meetings, mandatory training, check-ins), indicating modality, accessibility considerations, and points of contact.

Evaluate the HR metrics dashboard: using the provided dashboard/screenshots, assess fitness for purpose (coverage of turnover, absence, recruitment pipeline; definitions; data quality; timeliness; visual clarity; relevance to leadership decisions).
Draft recommendations: propose prioritized improvements with rationale (quick wins vs. longer-term changes) and any data or process changes required.
Prepare an in-class leadership presentation: 6–8 minutes to present dashboard evaluation findings and recommendations. Anticipate and prepare responses to two likely questions from leadership.
Participate in the peer-review workshop: exchange feedback with classmates on clarity, accessibility, and audit-readiness. Record key feedback and changes made.
Finalise and submit: print the portfolio for in-class submission and upload your presentation slides (PDF) to the LMS before your presentation slot.
deliverables: Audit-ready compliance pack: policy register; evidence logs; document control/version history; short summary note of gaps and mitigations.
Induction communications redesign: two revised templates; updated onboarding FAQ (up to 10 Q&As); inclusive induction schedule (2–4 weeks).

rubric.criterionName: Creation of an audit-ready compliance pack (registers, evidence logs, version-controlled documents)
rubric.fail: Compliance pack is incomplete or disorganised. Missing key elements (e.g., no policy register or evidence logs). No or incorrect version control. Documents are not traceable to owners/approvers. Significant inaccuracies or unredacted personal/confidential data present.
rubric.pass: Compliance pack includes a usable policy register, basic evidence logs, and a document control table with at least one approved version. Documents are appropriately redacted and traceable. Minor omissions or inconsistencies do not prevent audit sampling.
rubric.merit: Compliance pack is comprehensive and consistently structured. Policy register and evidence logs are cross-referenced and complete. Version control shows clear change history and approvals. Gaps are identified with practical mitigations. Ready for sampling with minimal auditor follow-up.
rubric.distinction: Compliance pack demonstrates exemplary audit readiness: fully traceable documents, rigorous versioning with approvals and change rationales, clear legal/regulatory mapping, and sampling-ready evidence logs. Proactive risk notes and corrective actions are prioritised and clearly documented.

rubric.criterionName: Analysis of onboarding feedback and redesign of induction communications and schedule for accessibility and inclusion
rubric.fail: Limited or no analysis of feedback. Redesign does not address identified issues or introduces inaccuracies. Communications are unclear or exclude key groups. Schedule is missing, impractical, or inaccessible.
rubric.pass: Feedback is analysed to identify main issues. Redesigned communications are clearer and address basic accessibility (readability, structure). Schedule is complete, logical, and signposts support and adjustments.
rubric.merit: Analysis is insightful with clear themes and evidence (e.g., frequencies, examples). Communications show inclusive language, improved timing, and multiple formats. Schedule integrates checkpoints, mandatory training, and reasonable adjustments with clear ownership.
rubric.distinction: Analysis is robust, segmented where relevant (e.g., role/department), and links issues to root causes. Communications demonstrate tested accessibility (readability level, alt text, plain-English design) and proactively address inclusion and FAQs. Schedule optimises flow, mitigates bottlenecks, and includes contingency for adjustments.

rubric.criterionName: Evaluation of HR metrics dashboard fitness for purpose and presentation of recommendations to leadership
rubric.fail: Evaluation is superficial or off-topic. Key metrics, definitions, or data issues are ignored. Recommendations are absent or not actionable. Presentation is unclear, significantly over/under time, or cannot answer basic questions.
rubric.pass: Evaluation addresses coverage, definitions, and basic data quality/visual clarity. Recommendations are relevant and actionable. Presentation is clear, within time, and handles straightforward questions.
rubric.merit: Evaluation is well-structured and evidence-based, critiquing relevance to leadership decisions, data integrity, and visual design. Recommendations are prioritised with rationale and expected benefits. Presentation is engaging, well-paced, and handles probing questions with appropriate justification.
rubric.distinction: Evaluation provides a balanced, critical appraisal against explicit fitness criteria (KPI definitions, timeliness, completeness, comparability, stakeholder needs). Recommendations include a staged roadmap (quick wins to longer-term), risks, and measures of success. Presentation is concise, persuasive, and demonstrates executive-level communication with confident, accurate Q&A.

All sources of help and information are acknowledged. Any use of tools for proofreading or formatting is declared.’

Examples include: extended time for the in-class presentation; presenting seated or via a recorded presentation if required; provision of large-print or dyslexia-friendly templates; acceptance of digital instead of printed portfolio where a print disability applies; quiet-room presentation slot; BSL interpreter or note-taker. Alternative formats must demonstrate the same learning outcomes and assessment standards (no reduction in academic requirements). All templates are screen-reader compatible. If you require adjustments, contact the module leader and Student Support at least one week before the presentation.

assessedOutcomes.mloStatement: Create an audit-ready compliance pack with policy register, evidence logs, and version-controlled documents for HR audit
Analyse onboarding feedback to redesign induction communications and schedule addressing accessibility and inclusion
Evaluate the HR metrics dashboard’s fitness for purpose and present improvement recommendations to leadership

brief.studentFacingIntro: This self-paced portfolio assesses your ability to produce an audit-ready HR compliance pack, use onboarding feedback to improve induction communications and schedules, and evaluate an HR metrics dashboard for leadership. You will work independently, submit all work digitally, and use the rubric and self-check prompts to validate quality before submission.
brief.workplaceContext: You are an HR Coordinator at a UK-based organisation preparing for an internal HR audit in six weeks. Recent onboarding feedback has highlighted issues with clarity and accessibility of induction communications. Leadership also wants confidence that the current HR metrics dashboard is fit for purpose and understands where to improve next. You will assemble a compliance pack, analyse onboarding feedback to redesign induction communications and schedules, and evaluate the HR metrics dashboard with recommendations for leadership.
stepByStepInstructions: Set up your working folder: Create a clear folder structure (e.g., 01_CompliancePack, 02_OnboardingAnalysis, 03_DashboardEvaluation, 04_Appendices). Use a consistent file naming convention (e.g., Surname_ID_Module_Assignment_v1.0).
Part A: Build the audit-ready compliance pack (MLO 1).

A1. Create a Policy Register (spreadsheet) including, at minimum: Policy/Procedure title, Owner, Version, Effective date, Review date, Status, Location/Link, Evidence reference(s), Related legislation/standard, Last reviewed by, Next action. Include a minimum of eight HR policies/procedures relevant to UK employment and HR operations.

A2. Compile Evidence Logs to demonstrate compliance (spreadsheets or forms). Include anonymised or synthetic entries for items such as right-to-work checks, policy acknowledgements, training completions, and document reviews. Cross-reference each entry to the Policy Register.

A3. Provide Version-Controlled Documents: Include at least two policy/procedure documents showing a document control section (version history, change summary, owner, approver, approval date, next review). Clearly indicate current version and archive prior versions or include a changes table.

A4. Create an Index and ReadMe: Add a one-page index that lists contents and where to find evidence. Include a ReadMe file describing folder structure, naming conventions, and any assumptions (no personal data).

Self-check for Part A: Does the register include all required fields? Are evidence items cross-referenced to policies? Do documents show version history and approvals? Is the pack navigable and logically structured?
Part B: Analyse onboarding feedback and redesign induction communications and schedule (MLO 2).

B1. Source or simulate onboarding feedback data (anonymised). If you do not have access to data, create a synthetic dataset of at least 20 responses with fields such as: clarity of communications (rating), usefulness of schedule (rating), accessibility experience (rating), top issues (multiple choice or free text), and open comments.

B2. Analyse the data: Summarise key quantitative results (e.g., averages, distributions) and identify qualitative themes from comments. Highlight issues linked to clarity, accessibility, inclusion, and timing.

B3. Redesign the induction communications: Draft a plain-English welcome email and a short FAQ or information sheet addressing common queries and accessibility needs (e.g., alternative formats, assistive tech compatibility, contact for adjustments).

B4. Redesign the induction schedule: Produce an inclusive, accessible schedule (e.g., first two weeks) that accounts for diverse needs (e.g., flexible timing, captioned/recorded sessions, accessible resources, quiet time for paperwork). Indicate delivery mode and links to resources.
B5. Produce a short commentary (within your report) mapping each redesign decision to specific feedback findings and explaining how accessibility and inclusion were addressed.

Self-check for Part B: Does the analysis combine quantitative and qualitative evidence? Are redesign choices traceable to findings? Are communications accessible (clear language, logical headings, readable contrast)? Does the schedule indicate adjustments and formats?
Part C: Evaluate the HR metrics dashboard and present recommendations (MLO 3).

C1. Define evaluation criteria suitable for leadership needs, such as: relevance and definitions of metrics (turnover, absence, recruitment pipeline), accuracy and data quality, timeliness/latency, segmentation, visual clarity/accessibility, and actionability.

C2. Evaluate the current or a representative HR metrics dashboard (use your workplace version or a constructed example based on typical HR metrics). Identify strengths, gaps, and risks aligned to your criteria.

C3. Develop 3–5 prioritised, evidence-based recommendations to improve the dashboard (e.g., add definitions, improve data refresh cadence, introduce segmentation, enhance accessibility). Indicate anticipated benefits, risks if not implemented, and effort/impact.

C4. Prepare leadership-facing materials: (i) a slide deck summarising evaluation findings and recommendations, and (ii) an 8–10 minute recorded presentation (voice-over slides is acceptable). Include an executive summary (one page) for quick reading.
Self-check for Part C: Are criteria explicit and used consistently? Do recommendations address leadership needs and feasibility? Is the recording clear, within time, and logically structured?
Final packaging and submission: Complete the self-checklist, ensure all files are named consistently, and export written materials to PDF where possible. Zip the full portfolio and upload to the LMS.
deliverables: Part A: Audit-ready compliance pack folder containing: Policy Register (spreadsheet), Evidence Logs (spreadsheets/forms), Version-controlled documents (at least two), Index and ReadMe.
Part B: Onboarding analysis and redesign pack containing: Analysis report (with findings and mapping to redesign), Accessible welcome email and FAQ/information sheet, Inclusive induction schedule.
Part C: Dashboard evaluation and recommendations containing: Slide deck, 8–10 minute recorded presentation, One-page executive summary.
Appendices: Synthetic/anonymised datasets used (CSV/XLSX), any analysis workings (optional).
Completed self-checklist (one page) confirming each requirement is met.

rubric.pass: All core components present and mostly accurate. Policy register includes required fields with minor gaps. Evidence logs are plausible and cross-referenced to relevant policies. Version control is evident on required documents. Folder structure and index enable basic navigation.
rubric.merit: Comprehensive, accurate register with clear ownership, dates, and legislative references. Evidence logs provide clear traceability and sampling sufficiency. Version histories include change summaries and approvals. Pack is logically structured with an informative index and ReadMe, demonstrating audit readiness.
rubric.distinction: Professional, audit-ready pack demonstrating complete traceability and robust document control. Consistent metadata across artefacts, clear review cycles, and ownership. Evidence triangulates policy to proof with no critical errors. Navigation, naming conventions, and signposting enable rapid audit sampling.

Communications apply plain English and accessible formatting. Schedule is realistic, inclusive, and clearly signposts adjustments and resource formats.

Recommendations are prioritised with rationale and anticipated benefits/risks. Slides and delivery present a clear, persuasive narrative for leadership.
rubric.distinction: Rigorous evaluation referencing good practice/benchmarks and quantifying issues where appropriate. Recommendations form a compelling, prioritised roadmap addressing impact, effort, and risks (including data governance and accessibility). brief.workplaceContext: You are the HR coordinator in a UK organisation preparing for an external HR audit while responding to recent onboarding feedback and upcoming leadership review of the HR metrics dashboard. You must compile an audit-ready compliance pack, redesign induction communications and schedule to address accessibility and inclusion, and evaluate the current HR dashboard to recommend actionable improvements.
stepByStepInstructions: Confirm your data source: workplace documents (with permission and redaction) or the provided case pack. Ensure no personal data is exposed.

Build the compliance pack: create a policy register (title, owner, version, approval date, next review, location), evidence logs (what, where, who, date, control), and assemble version-controlled policy documents (consistent naming, version history, approvals).
Quality-check the compliance pack: check completeness against the template checklist; ensure traceability from register to evidence; verify version control and review dates.
Gather onboarding feedback: collate survey results, FAQs, emails, and exit/induction comments from the case pack or workplace sources; anonymise as needed.
Analyse onboarding feedback: identify key themes and pain points; quantify where possible (e.g., counts/percentages); consider different groups’ needs; surface accessibility and inclusion issues.

Redesign induction communications and schedule: draft clear, inclusive messages (plain English, readable layout, alternative formats) and a practical induction schedule with timings, responsibilities, and accessible delivery options.

Evaluate the HR metrics dashboard: define fitness-for-purpose criteria (e.g., relevance, validity, timeliness, accessibility, actionability for leadership); assess current dashboard against criteria with evidence (screenshots, data notes, user comments).
Recommend improvements: propose prioritised, feasible enhancements to metrics, visuals, and cadence; include quick wins and a short roadmap; explain expected benefits and any risks.

Prepare a leadership presentation: 6–8 minutes with slides summarising the evaluation, key findings, and recommendations; deliver live in class/online or submit a recording with captions or transcript.

Compile and submit the portfolio: include a contents page, the compliance pack, onboarding analysis and redesign, dashboard evaluation with recommendations, and presentation slides/recording link or file; submit via LMS as a single ZIP/PDF or provide a physical folder if needed.

Onboarding analysis report and redesigned induction communications and schedule addressing accessibility and inclusion.
Dashboard evaluation report with improvement recommendations for leadership, including annotated screenshots or mock-ups.
Leadership presentation: slides and either a recording (MP4) or confirmation of live delivery with a recording uploaded.

rubric.criterionName: Create an audit-ready compliance pack
rubric.fail: Pack is incomplete or disorganised; policy register and/or evidence logs missing or inaccurate; version control not demonstrated; documents lack approvals or review dates; data protection breaches or unredacted personal data present; not audit-ready.
rubric.pass: Pack includes a policy register, evidence logs, and version-controlled documents; basic traceability from register to evidence; consistent naming and versioning used; minor gaps/errors that do not prevent audit use; personal data appropriately redacted.
rubric.merit: Pack is robust and clearly structured; comprehensive register with owners, approvals, and review cycle; evidence logs provide a reliable trail; version history shows approvals and changes; alignment with UK employment compliance is evident; no data protection issues.
rubric.distinction: Pack is exemplary and audit-ready without rework; complete, accurate, and fully traceable artefacts with cross-references; rigorous version control (metadata, approvals, change notes); proactive gap identification and mitigation documented; demonstrates readiness for external audit.

rubric.criterionName: Analyse onboarding feedback and redesign induction communications and schedule

rubric.merit: Systematic analysis integrates qualitative themes with quantitative indicators; insights are segmented where appropriate; redesigned communications demonstrate inclusive language, structure, and formats; schedule improves flow and access (e.g., flexible options, support for different needs).
rubric.distinction: Insightful, evidence-led analysis with triangulation across sources; clear rationale linking findings to redesign choices; communications and schedule exemplify accessibility and inclusion (e.g., readability, multiple formats, clear ownership, inclusive timing); measurable improvement goals are defined.

rubric.criterionName: Evaluate HR metrics dashboard and present recommendations to leadership

rubric.merit: Evaluation uses well-defined, weighted criteria (e.g., validity, timeliness, actionability, accessibility); trade-offs and limitations are considered; recommendations are prioritised with impact/effort rationale; presentation is professional, logically structured, and audience-focused.
rubric.distinction: Critical, balanced evaluation integrating user feedback and data quality considerations; risks and dependencies are articulated; recommendations include a short roadmap and mock-ups with expected benefits; presentation is compelling and anticipates leadership questions with evidence-based responses.

overview.examPurpose: Validate program-level competence across all PLOs

sectionA.questionText: You are updating a new starter’s HRIS record after receiving a deed poll for a legal name change. To maintain accuracy while meeting UK GDPR principles, which control is most appropriate?
options: A) Enable employee self-service to update legal name with mandatory evidence upload, field validation, and an audit trail requiring HR approval before commit.
B) Ask the line manager to email the new name and update the record immediately without evidence to avoid delays.
C) Update the HRIS and keep a permanent copy of all supporting documents, including utilities, regardless of retention rules.
D) Create a parallel spreadsheet of changes and reconcile monthly to avoid altering the HRIS directly.
sectionA.rationale: Employee self-service with validation, evidence, approval and audit trail supports accuracy, data minimisation and accountability under UK GDPR while ensuring controlled HRIS updates.

sectionA.questionText: A remote candidate provides a Home Office share code for a right to work check before starting. What is the compliant action to obtain a statutory excuse?
options: A) Use the Home Office online service with the share code and candidate’s DOB, verify likeness via live video, and retain a dated copy of the online profile page.
B) Accept a scanned passport sent by email and keep it in the HR shared drive.
C) Delay the right to work check until the candidate’s first payday to avoid delays in onboarding.
D) Ask for the candidate’s National Insurance number and keep this as evidence of right to work.
sectionA.rationale: For online checks, employers must confirm identity and retain evidence from the Home Office service with the date of check to establish a statutory excuse.

sectionA.questionText: A new starter has no P45. What should you do to set them up correctly for payroll?
options: A) Ask the employee to complete the HMRC starter checklist and apply the resulting starter declaration and tax code per HMRC guidance.
B) Apply tax code 0T on a cumulative basis until HMRC writes to you.
C) Wait for the employee’s first payslip before assigning a tax code.
D) Use the same tax code as their colleague in a similar role.
sectionA.rationale: The HMRC starter checklist replaces the P46 and determines the correct starter declaration and initial tax code.

sectionA.questionText: You are standardising turnover reporting across departments of different sizes. Which approach best supports fair comparison on the dashboard?
options: A) Monthly turnover rate using average headcount for the period as the denominator.
B) Number of leavers compared to end-of-month headcount.
C) Cumulative annual leavers displayed as a simple count.
D) Total leavers divided by budgeted headcount at year start.
sectionA.rationale: Normalising by average headcount ensures comparability of turnover across units of different sizes and reduces denominator bias.

sectionA.questionText: A manager wants to extend a probation period and ‘pause’ statutory holiday accrual during the extension. Identify the key compliance risk.
options: A) Statutory holiday under the Working Time Regulations accrues from day one; accrual cannot be paused, though taking leave can be managed.
B) Holiday only accrues after successful probation, so pausing accrual is compliant.
C) Holiday accrual rules are a matter of company discretion with no statutory baseline.
D) Pausing accrual is allowed provided the employee signs an addendum.
sectionA.rationale: Statutory holiday accrues from day one; employers can manage when leave is taken but not stop accrual. Probation extensions also require contractual basis and compliant notice.

sectionA.questionText: A draft Day 1 induction email says: “Be in the office at 09:00 in smart dress. We’ll sort your IT then.” Provide two specific edits to make this clearer and more inclusive for diverse new starters.
sectionA.correctAnswer: Examples: 1) Specify location or meeting link, contact person, and accessibility arrangements (e.g., step-free access, captioning). 2) Replace vague ‘smart dress’ with inclusive guidance (e.g., ‘smart casual; religious/cultural dress welcomed’) and include a brief schedule with breaks and what to bring (ID for RTW, if applicable).
sectionA.rationale: Clarity on logistics and inclusive language reduces ambiguity, supports accessibility, and sets expectations appropriate for diverse hires.

sectionA.questionText: You discover a live HR shared folder holding recruitment files (IDs, CVs) for candidates rejected 24 months ago. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: A) Apply the recruitment data retention schedule: delete or anonymise records beyond retention, document the disposal, and prevent future overspill (e.g., auto-archiving controls).
B) Keep all files indefinitely in case any candidate reapplies.
C) Move the files to a manager’s personal drive to reduce visibility.
D) Email all rejected candidates to request new consent to keep their data forever.
sectionA.rationale: UK GDPR requires storage limitation and documented retention. Applying the schedule and strengthening controls addresses compliance and governance.

sectionA.questionText: An interview panel has limited availability next week; the candidate requests 48 hours’ notice and asks about reasonable adjustments. What is the best scheduling action?
options: A) Offer two or three time slots that meet the notice period, confirm any adjustments, send calendar invites with the interview pack and access details, and log adjustments for the panel.
B) Book the only slot the panel can do and tell the candidate to rearrange their commitments.
C) Ask the candidate to call reception on arrival and decide adjustments on the day.
D) Cancel the interview and withdraw the application due to scheduling constraints.
sectionA.rationale: Providing options that respect notice, confirming adjustments, and sharing packs aligns with fair and efficient recruitment logistics and equality duties.

sectionA.questionText: An employee’s salary increases from £3,000 to £3,300 effective 15th of a 30-day month. Using calendar day pro‑rata, what is the gross salary for that month?
sectionA.rationale: Half month at £3,000 (£1,500) plus half month at £3,300 (£1,650) totals £3,150.

sectionA.questionText: A full-time employee reports sickness Monday–Thursday and returns Friday. Qualifying days are Monday–Friday. Assuming eligibility, how should payroll process SSP?
options: A) Pay SSP for one day (day 4), and ensure the absence is coded correctly.
B) Pay SSP for all four days.
C) Do not pay SSP because the absence is under a week.
D) Deduct a full week of salary and pay no SSP.
sectionA.rationale: SSP is payable from the 4th qualifying day in a PIW; the first three are waiting days.

sectionA.questionText: Your recruitment dashboard shows counts at each pipeline stage, but hiring managers cannot see where candidates are dropping out. What change best improves insight?
options: A) Display stage-to-stage conversion rates and time-in-stage, cohorting by requisition month.
B) Keep total counts but sort by candidate surname.
C) Replace charts with a narrative paragraph per requisition.
D) Show a pie chart of total applicants by department.
sectionA.rationale: Conversion rates and time-in-stage, segmented by cohort, reveal funnel leaks and bottlenecks more effectively than raw counts.

sectionA.questionText: For policy documentation under audit, name three specific elements of version control and governance that must be present on the document.
sectionA.correctAnswer: Any three of: version number; document owner; approver; approval date; effective date; next review date; change log/summary of changes; document ID; controlled location.
sectionA.rationale: Clear versioning and governance metadata provide traceability and assurance for audits.

sectionA.questionText: For a British passport holder completing pre‑employment checks remotely via a certified Identity Service Provider (IDSP), which step is required to maintain a statutory excuse?
options: A) Obtain the IDSP output showing image and verification outcome, confirm the person’s likeness via live video or in‑person, and retain dated evidence.
B) Accept an emailed passport scan without further checks and store it in any shared folder.
C) Skip the check because British citizens do not require right to work verification.
D) Ask the candidate’s manager to approve employment without documentation.
sectionA.rationale: Using an IDSP requires employer confirmation of identity (likeness) and retention of evidence to establish the statutory excuse.

sectionA.questionText: An employee asks HR to delete an active disciplinary warning from their HRIS record, citing the ‘right to be forgotten’. How should you respond to remain compliant?
sectionA.correctAnswer: Explain that erasure does not apply where data must be retained for legitimate interests/legal obligations; ensure the record is accurate, access-restricted, retained only per the retention schedule, and advise the employee of their rights (e.g., to complain to the DPO/ICO).
sectionA.rationale: Active disciplinary data may be retained lawfully with strict access and defined retention; transparency about rights is required.

sectionA.questionText: Onboarding feedback shows Day 1 had five back‑to‑back sessions, no breaks, and new starters missed a security briefing due to IT access delays. What is the best action to improve inclusivity and clarity?
options: A) Re‑sequence the schedule to include buffer times and breaks, send the agenda and access checks in advance, and provide recorded/captioned content with a clear point of contact.
B) Shorten all sessions by 5 minutes without changing the order.
C) Ask managers to remind new starters to arrive earlier.
D) Remove the security briefing from Day 1.
sectionA.rationale: Proactive scheduling, pre‑checks, and accessible materials improve comprehension and inclusion and reduce first‑day failures.

sectionA.questionText: In April, a department recorded 64 sickness days against 1,600 scheduled workdays. What is the sickness absence rate for the dashboard?
sectionA.rationale: Absence rate = sickness days / scheduled days = 64/1600 = 0.04 = 4.0%.

sectionA.questionText: A new starter was added after payroll cut‑off. What is the best compliant approach to avoid undue delay in pay?
options: A) Process an approved off‑cycle/advance payment per policy and include the employee in the next payroll, ensuring statutory deductions are handled correctly.
B) Wait until next month’s payroll with no communication to the employee.
C) Ask the manager to pay cash and reclaim later.
D) Add the employee twice in the next run to ‘catch up’ automatically.
sectionA.rationale: Off‑cycle payments under control mitigate hardship while preserving payroll compliance and audit trail.

sectionA.questionText: New‑starter FAQs show repeated confusion about first payday and benefits enrolment deadlines. Draft two concise FAQ entries that address these points clearly.
sectionA.correctAnswer: Examples: 1) ‘When is my first payday?’ Your first payday is the last working day of the month. If you start after the payroll cut‑off (15th), you will receive an advance per policy and the balance in the next cycle. 2) ‘When must I enrol in benefits?’ You have 30 days from your start date to enrol via the benefits portal; after this window, changes may be restricted. Links and contacts provided.
sectionA.rationale: Clear, time‑bound instructions reduce queries and support equitable access to pay and benefits.

sectionC.taskDescription: Design and justify an HR metrics dashboard and executive commentary for departmental reporting. You are provided with anonymised monthly datasets (24 months) covering headcount, leavers by department, absence events by reason, and recruitment pipeline stages for a UK SME. Create a dashboard specification and evaluate the trends to prioritise operational actions.
instructions: Interrogate the datasets. Calculate at minimum: monthly turnover %, 12‑month rolling turnover, monthly absence rate % and average days lost per FTE, recruitment time‑to‑hire, stage conversion rates, and offer acceptance rate. State any assumptions.
Select 6–8 metrics for the dashboard that best explain turnover, absence, and pipeline health. Justify your selections in relation to decision‑making needs of department heads.
Sketch a wireframe (describe layout) specifying chart types, labels, time windows, and RAG thresholds for each KPI. Include a brief data quality note (source, refresh, validation checks).
Write a 300–350 word executive commentary identifying 3–4 key trends or risks, with plausible root causes supported by the data.
Create a one‑page action plan with 3 targeted interventions, named owners, timelines, and 2 SMART KPIs to track impact over the next quarter.
sectionC.modelAnswer:
Expected approach and key elements:
- Calculations: Monthly turnover % = leavers in month / average headcount in month; rolling 12‑month turnover; absence rate % = total absence days / (available workdays × FTE); average days lost per FTE; recruitment time‑to‑hire (req approval to acceptance); stage conversion rates; offer acceptance rate.
- Dashboard metrics (example): Headcount; monthly and 12‑month rolling turnover (overall and by department); absence rate % and 12‑month rolling; absence reasons distribution; time‑to‑hire (median and 75th percentile); funnel with stage conversions; offer acceptance rate; open vacancies aging. Optional: Bradford Factor at team level, not individual.
- Wireframe: Top row KPI tiles (Headcount, Turnover %, Absence %, Time‑to‑hire, Offer acceptance). Left panel: 24‑month lines for turnover and absence with RAG bands (e.g., Turnover >18% red, 12–18% amber, <12% green). Right panel: Recruitment funnel chart with conversion rates; bar chart of absence reasons. Footer: data notes (source: HRIS, ATS; refresh: monthly; validations: reconcile headcount to payroll, duplicate ID checks, date logic).
- Insights (illustrative): Q1 spike in short‑term sickness drives absence from 3.1% to 4.6%; Sales turnover rolling rate at 22% vs company 15%, coinciding with below‑market OTE; Time‑to‑hire inflated (median 38 days) due to long manager review stage; Offer acceptance dipped to 71% in last quarter as competing offers increased.
- Actions: (1) Implement manager SLAs and ATS nudges to reduce review stage by 5 days; (2) Targeted retention in Sales (comp review, career paths); (3) Health and wellbeing intervention plus RTW conversations to curb short‑term sickness. Owners named, timelines 90 days.
- SMART KPIs: Reduce median time‑to‑hire from 38 to 28 days within 90 days; Lower absence rate from 4.6% to ≤3.8% within 6 months; Improve offer acceptance from 71% to ≥82% next quarter. Include monitoring plan and data quality controls.
assessmentCriteria: Appropriate metric selection and justified alignment to decision needs
Accuracy of calculations and correct interpretation of trends
Clarity and usability of dashboard design, including RAG thresholds and data governance notes
Quality, feasibility, and ownership of the action plan
Specificity and measurability of proposed KPIs and monitoring approach

sectionC.taskDescription: Evaluate compliance risks across UK pre‑employment, HRIS data protection, payroll, and leave processes, then create a version‑controlled policy amendment pack and audit evidence plan for an external audit scheduled in four weeks.
instructions: Using the provided process summaries and current policies (Right to Work, Data Retention, Sickness Absence, Family Leave, Payroll Cut‑offs), identify 8–12 discrete compliance risks. Rate likelihood and impact (High/Med/Low) and provide evidence‑based rationales, citing UK legal sources.

Draft a policy amendment summary (one page per policy) with version control metadata (version, date, author, approver, change summary, next review date) and specific tracked‑change recommendations to mitigate the identified risks.

Produce a one‑page audit evidence plan listing artefacts to obtain, sample sizes and periods, owners, and the test procedure for each risk area (e.g., RTW sampling, holiday pay calculation check, data retention purge logs).
Prioritise three critical risks and justify the order of remediation considering regulatory exposure and business impact.
sectionC.modelAnswer:
Expected approach and key elements:
- Risks (examples) with mapping: (1) RTW checks not completed before start or inadequate copies retained – Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006/HO RTW guidance; (2) Missing re‑checks for limited leave to remain – same; (3) Personal data retained beyond stated periods or stored in email – UK GDPR/Data Protection Act 2018 (Art.5 storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality); (4) Lack of DPIA for new HRIS integration; (5) Holiday pay excludes regular overtime/commission – Working Time Regulations 1998 case law; (6) Payroll cut‑off causing underpayment for starters/changes – ERA 1996 unlawful deduction risk; (7) Inaccessible family leave policy wording risking indirect discrimination – Equality Act 2010; (8) Failure to issue day‑one written statement particulars – ERA 1996 s.1; (9) Inaccurate absence recording undermining SSP eligibility – SSP Regs; (10) Insecure passport scans shared via email – UK GDPR Art.32.
- Ratings justified with context (e.g., evidence of late RTW from sample logs; known grievances about holiday pay). Include RAG and brief controls.
- Policy amendments: Insert explicit RTW process (in‑person or IDVT/online share code), documented copy requirements, and re‑check triggers; retention schedule table (e.g., RTW copies retained for duration of employment + 2 years), secure storage, purge cadence, and access controls; holiday pay calculation rule to include regular overtime/commission with reference period; payroll change cut‑off escalation and retro process; accessible language and equality impact statement; add version control block (v2.3, dd/mm/yyyy, author, approver, next review in 12 months).
- Audit evidence plan: Artefacts and sampling (e.g., RTW: 25 starters in last 6 months, verify date of check before start, document quality, follow‑up on limited leave; Holiday pay: 30 employees with overtime over last 12 weeks, recalculate; Data retention: purge logs and access logs for HRIS; Payroll: audit trail of changes vs. payslips; Policies: approval records, distribution proof, training logs). Assign owners and test steps.
- Prioritisation: 1) RTW pre‑employment legality (civil penalty and criminal exposure) – remediate immediately; 2) Holiday pay underpayment (financial and tribunal risk) – urgent correction and back‑pay review; 3) Data retention/security (ICO enforcement risk) – initiate DPIA, implement purge and secure workflows.
assessmentCriteria: Comprehensive identification of risks with correct UK legal mapping and defensible ratings
Quality and specificity of mitigations embedded in policy amendments with robust version control
Practicality and sufficiency of the audit evidence plan (artefacts, sampling, owners, procedures)
Sound justification for remediation prioritisation balancing regulatory and business risk
Clarity, concision, and professional presentation suitable for audit

sectionC.taskDescription: Create an inclusive induction communications pack and schedule using onboarding feedback and FAQs. Evaluate themes from the provided feedback set, then design communications and a measurement plan to improve new starter experience in the UK context.
instructions: Analyse the feedback and FAQs to identify 4–6 themes affecting clarity, inclusion, and readiness (e.g., system access delays, RTW documentation confusion, first payday expectations, reasonable adjustments). Summarise each theme with supporting evidence.

Draft: (a) a welcome email template (200–250 words) with placeholders, (b) a detailed Day‑1 and Week‑1 schedule (timed activities, owners, outcomes), and (c) an updated FAQ (10–12 items) addressing pain points, including RTW checks and payroll setup steps.

Embed inclusive design features: plain language, consistent headings, accessibility notes (e.g., alt‑text, readable fonts, captioned media), and options for reasonable adjustments. Specify delivery channels and timing (pre‑start, Day‑1, end of Week‑1) including reminders.
Define a lightweight version control and review cadence (naming, versioning, approver, change log, review cycle) and a plan to evaluate effectiveness (3–4 metrics, feedback loop, and A/B test idea).
sectionC.modelAnswer:
Expected approach and key elements:
- Thematic analysis (examples): Unclear start‑day logistics; confusion on RTW documents still needed (e.g., share code vs. physical documents); delays in laptop/system access; uncertainty about first payday and benefits windows; lack of clarity on hybrid working and reasonable adjustments. Evidence cited from feedback percentages/comments.
- Communications:
  a) Welcome email template: Friendly, plain English; includes start date/time, location/Teams link, dress guidance, what to bring (only if RTW pending), who to contact, accessibility options, links to pre‑start tasks (HRIS account, bank details, RTW upload), and privacy notice link. Placeholders for names, dates, links.
  b) Day‑1 schedule: Manager check‑in; RTW verification slot; HR induction (policies, payroll, benefits); IT setup with service desk; buddy lunch; e‑learning accessibility brief. Week‑1: team introductions, safety training, role onboarding milestones, shadowing, end‑of‑week check‑in.
  c) FAQ items: RTW evidence types (e.g., Home Office share code process), deadline for completing pre‑start tasks, when first pay is received, expense process, how to request adjustments, hybrid working expectations, benefits enrolment windows, who to contact for IT, how to access HRIS, where to find policies.
- Inclusive design: Reading age ~B1, short paragraphs, descriptive link text, alt‑text guidance for any attachments, captioned videos, dyslexia‑friendly font guidance, colour‑contrast compliant palette, offer of large‑print/alternative formats, time‑zone considerate meeting times for remote staff.
- Delivery plan: Pre‑start email T‑7 days with calendar invites; SMS/ATS reminder T‑3 days for outstanding tasks; Day‑1 printed/digital schedule; Week‑1 wrap‑up message with quick survey link.
- Version control: Document title with semantic versioning (e.g., Induction_Pack_v1.0_ddmmyyyy), author and approver named, change log table, next review in 6 months or upon legal/policy change.
- Measurement: New starter CSAT at Day‑5 and Day‑30; completion rate and time for pre‑start tasks; time‑to‑system‑access ≤24 hours; 90‑day early attrition trend. A/B test subject lines and sending times to improve pre‑start open/click rates, and compare CSAT outcomes.
assessmentCriteria: Insightful synthesis of feedback into actionable themes
Clarity, accuracy, and inclusivity of the drafted communications and schedules
Coverage and correctness of FAQs for UK onboarding and RTW context
Robustness of delivery, version control, and review arrangements
Feasible, relevant metrics and feedback mechanisms demonstrating a test‑and‑learn approach

sectionC.modelAnswer: Design a multi‑level HR metrics dashboard with standardised definitions and executive commentary. 1) Governance and audience: define purpose (operational vs executive), cadence (monthly/quarterly), and owners. 2) Standard definitions: publish metric dictionary (e.g., headcount point‑in‑time; FTE; starters/leavers; turnover as leavers/average headcount × 100; vacancy rate; time‑to‑hire; offer acceptance; DEI representation; absence rate; L&D hours; engagement index; internal mobility; pay equity indices). 3) Metric set: a) Workforce: headcount/FTE, joins/leavers, voluntary turnover (12‑month rolling), vacancy rate, span of control; b) Talent acquisition: applicants per hire, qualified‑applicant rate, stage conversion, time‑to‑hire and time‑in‑stage, cost‑per‑hire, offer acceptance; c) DEI: representation by grade, hire/promotion rates by protected characteristic, gender/ethnicity pay differentials; d) Absence and wellbeing: absence rate, Bradford Factor, mental health days, EAP utilisation; e) Performance and mobility: performance distribution, promotions, lateral moves, talent risk/bench strength; f) Capability and learning: training hours per FTE, completion/compliance rates, time to productivity; g) Reward: compa‑ratio, pay progression, bonus coverage; h) Employee relations: case volumes, resolution time; i) Retention risks: regretted loss rate, tenure distribution. 4) Design principles: segment by department, location, grade; show trend vs target/benchmark; use rolling averages; visualise with funnels for TA, heatmaps for DEI, control charts for stability; include data quality indicators. 5) Executive commentary: for each domain, summarise key movements, drivers (internal/external), hotspot analysis, risks/opportunities, and specific, time‑bound actions with owners; link to strategic objectives and financial impact (e.g., vacancy cost, productivity). 6) Data pipeline: single source of truth (HRIS/ATS/LMS/payroll), ETL with data validation, privacy by design, role‑based access, and an agreed change log for definitions. 7) Cadence and review: monthly pack with quarterly deep dives; action tracking; continuous improvement based on stakeholder feedback.
sectionC.markAllocation: 20 marks total: 6 marks for a coherent, strategically aligned metric set with clear definitions and standardisation; 4 marks for segmentation, comparability, and visual design choices (trends, benchmarks, funnels/heatmaps/control charts); 5 marks for incisive executive commentary that explains drivers, quantifies impact, and specifies actions/owners; 3 marks for data governance and pipeline (sources, validation, RACI, access controls); 2 marks for cadence, action tracking, and continuous improvement.

performanceThresholds.pass: Provides a sensible core set of metrics with basic definitions and simple commentary; some segmentation or trends present.
performanceThresholds.merit: As pass, plus robust standardisation, clear visuals with benchmarks, and commentary that links insights to actions and owners; addresses data quality and access.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Demonstrates a fully integrated design with strategic line‑of‑sight, advanced segmentation and visualisation, quantified business impact, strong governance (data dictionary, access, QA), and an implementation cadence with action tracking.

sectionC.modelAnswer: Provide a structured risk evaluation across UK pre‑employment, HRIS data protection, payroll, and time off/holiday. 1) Pre‑employment and RTW: risks include unlawful discrimination in selection, conducting non‑compliant RTW checks (e.g., relying on photocopies or invalid share codes), ignoring time‑limited permissions, and misusing criminal records. Controls: standardised, role‑relevant selection criteria and training; compliant RTW (Home Office online checks for share codes; certified IDSP or in‑person for British/Irish passports); recordkeeping of checks and diarised repeats; DBS only where lawful and proportionate; documented adverse action process. 2) HRIS data protection (UK GDPR/DPA 2018): risks include over‑collection, unclear lawful bases, excessive retention, weak access controls, insecure sharing with processors, cross‑border transfers without safeguards, poor SAR handling, and lack of DPIAs for high‑risk processing (monitoring/biometrics). Controls: data minimisation and purpose limitation; RoPA; privacy notices; DPIAs; role‑based access and MFA; processor due diligence and DPAs; UK IDTA/SCCs for transfers; encryption and secure disposal; retention schedules; SAR workflow and redaction standards; incident response with breach assessment and ICO reporting where required. 3) Payroll and tax: risks include incorrect starter tax codes (no Starter Checklist), RTI submission failures, NMW/NLW breaches (including deductions, uniform, travel time), auto‑enrolment failures (eligibility, postponement notices, re‑enrolment), miscalculated holiday pay (especially for irregular hours/part‑year), SSP/SMP/SPP errors, benefits‑in‑kind reporting (P11D/payrolling) gaps, and off‑payroll working (IR35) misclassification. Controls: documented payroll controls and checklists; dual review; RTI timeliness; NMW monitoring including salary sacrifice impacts; robust auto‑enrolment processes (assessments, communications, contributions reconciliation, re‑enrolment tri‑annual); holiday pay calculations aligned to WTR and current case law/regulations; statutory pay calculators and evidence capture; P11D/payrolling policy and deadlines; IR35 assessments and SDS. 4) Time off and holiday: risks include not accruing statutory holiday during probation or leave, failing to carry over where applicable (e.g., sickness, family leave), unlawful rolled‑up holiday for non‑eligible workers, and inflexible policies disadvantaging protected groups. Controls: clear policies reflecting current regulations (including any permitted rolled‑up holiday for irregular/part‑year workers), tracking systems, manager training, and regular audits. 5) Monitoring and assurance: implement KPIs (e.g., RTW compliance rate, SAR turnaround, NMW exception reports), internal audits, corrective action plans, and Board reporting; maintain training logs and periodic policy reviews.
sectionC.markAllocation: 20 marks total: 6 marks for comprehensive identification of risks across the four domains with UK context; 6 marks for specific, proportionate controls aligned to law and guidance; 4 marks for implementation detail (processes, roles, records, and evidence); 2 marks for monitoring/audit and KPIs; 2 marks for currency with UK rules (e.g., RTW/IDSP, holiday pay, auto‑enrolment, NMW nuances).

performanceThresholds.fail: Superficial list of generic risks with few or no UK‑specific controls; lacks implementable steps.
performanceThresholds.pass: Identifies main risks and suggests appropriate basic controls in each area.
performanceThresholds.merit: As pass, plus provides concrete processes, roles, and evidence requirements; integrates monitoring/audit.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Presents a rigorous, UK‑specific risk/control framework with prioritisation, clear ownership, metrics, and up‑to‑date legal nuances; shows how assurance will operate in practice.

Sharing, reproducing, circulating, or soliciting assessment content (including screenshots or solution outlines) during or after the assessment window is strictly forbidden. Submissions may be subject to similarity checking, authorship and metadata analysis, and other forensic measures. Proven breaches may result in penalties up to and including a mark of zero, failure of the module, and disciplinary action, with due process and the right of appeal observed.

Identity verification: Students must access the assessment using institutional credentials and multi-factor authentication. Do not share login details or allow others to access your account. You may be required to complete a declaration of authorship, respond to spot-check identity queries, attend a short viva verification, or present a valid photo ID on request. System logs (e.g., IP, device, timestamp) are retained to support verification. Where remote proctoring or camera use is required, this will be proportionate, privacy-aware, compatible with approved adjustments, and notified in advance; alternative verification routes will be provided where necessary.

Online randomisation and scenario rotation: To protect assessment integrity while ensuring equivalence, items are delivered from calibrated pools mapped to the assessment blueprint. Each candidate receives: a randomised selection of items covering the same learning outcomes; shuffled item order; and, where applicable, rotated case vignettes or parameterised datasets of equivalent difficulty and marking weight. For objective items, response options are shuffled. For constructed responses, scenario variants are rotated across the cohort and between reassessment windows. Retakes draw from fresh pools. Exposure controls limit repeat presentation of the same content. Any downloadable materials may be watermarked with candidate identifiers. The system enforces the official time window and submission deadlines, records an audit trail, and locks responses upon expiry. Navigation controls (e.g., backtracking) will follow the settings stated in the brief.

Assessment conduct: Candidates must work alone in a quiet space, ensuring that no other person provides assistance or observes restricted content. Communication with others about the assessment is prohibited for the duration of the assessment window. Do not copy, print, or capture the assessment content. Save work regularly and submit before the deadline; late submissions follow the University policy. Academic queries on content cannot be answered during the window; technical issues must be reported promptly via the designated support channel with evidence (e.g., screenshots, error messages).

Data protection and security: Assessment data, logs, and any recordings are processed in accordance with UK GDPR and University data protection policies, stored securely, and retained only for legitimate academic and regulatory purposes within stated retention periods.
step13.accessibilityProvisions:
The University is committed to inclusive assessment in line with the Equality Act 2010 and anticipatory reasonable adjustment duties. Adjustments enable equitable demonstration of learning without lowering academic standards or altering competence standards. All provisions below apply to TEST 2 CHRP and the online self-study delivery mode, subject to confirmation by an approved Learning Support Plan (or equivalent) and the assessment brief.

Time-related adjustments: For any timed components, students with approved adjustments will receive additional time (for example, 25% or as specified), with separate, non-penalising rest breaks where indicated. Where appropriate, take-home elements may have extended submission windows, or alternative pacing, consistent with competence standards. In the event of verified technical disruption, a stop-the-clock or contingency resubmission may be applied in line with University policy. The assessment platform will provide visible timers and warnings that are compatible with assistive technologies.

Alternative formats and accessible design: Assessment materials will be provided in accessible formats (e.g., structured HTML or tagged PDF and, where feasible, Word versions) with clear headings, logical reading order, alt text for images, colour-independent cues, adequate contrast, and plain English instructions. Embedded media will include captions and transcripts. Large-print versions and high-contrast styles are available on request; tactile or Braille formats can be arranged with sufficient notice. Interactions that demand drag-and-drop or fine motor precision will have keyboard-accessible alternatives. Any equations, figures, or tables will be presented in screen-reader friendly formats where practicable.

Assistive technology allowances: Students may use approved assistive technologies such as screen readers (e.g., NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver), magnification tools, dictation/speech-to-text, screen overlays, ergonomic peripherals, and spelling or grammar support where these are not themselves the competence standard being assessed. Where calculation is not the competence standard, a basic calculator may be permitted. If identity verification or proctoring is required, it will be configured to be compatible with assistive technologies; where this is not feasible, an alternative verification method (for example, a post-assessment viva) will be provided. Remote reader or scribe support and BSL interpretation for instructions can be arranged by prior agreement.

Procedures and responsibilities: Students seeking adjustments should confirm their needs via the Disability or Wellbeing Service and the Programme Team at least 10 working days in advance of the assessment window, providing relevant evidence where required. Emergency adjustments for unforeseen circumstances will be considered under existing University policies. All personal data related to adjustments will be handled confidentially in line with UK GDPR.

No reduction of standards: Adjustments alter the means of demonstrating achievement, not the academic or professional standards being assessed. Learning outcomes, marking criteria, and any competence standards remain unchanged. Exemptions from spelling, grammar, or formatting will only apply where these are not core to the competence being assessed and where explicitly approved in the Learning Support Plan.
